Ground mismatch: WAS are run-first (38% pass when leading) into a DAL front that bleeds 133 rush yds/game and 0.62 RB1 rushing scores. Jacory Croskey-Merritt is a centerpiece.

The DAL host the WAS as favorites of 4.5, with the total set at 51.5 — a market that implies a DAL 28–24 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 33% of its snaps with DAL in front, 42% within one score, and 25% with DAL chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

A modest edge to DAL. They should lead more often than not, tilting them slightly toward the run late, while WAS leans a touch more pass-heavy to stay in it — but the effect is gentle; this isn't a script that dramatically reshapes anyone's usage.

The Key Matchups

WAS are soft against the run (143 yds/game allowed), and DAL feed Javonte Williams a heavy 62% carry share — a rushing-yards spot.

Jayden Daniels adds rushing value — he scrambles on 6.7% of dropbacks, live for rush-yard and anytime-TD props.

Efficiency edge to WAS — a 47% success-rate offense against a DAL defense that allows 47% — points should come.

Jayden Daniels has a passing-yards tailwind — DAL allow 252 pass yds/game (vs ~230).

CeeDee Lamb draws a plus matchup — WAS concede 68 yds/game to WR1s (league ~58), and DAL funnel 24% of targets his way. A rec-yards spot.

Sneaky value on Stefon Diggs (WR2) — DAL leak 43 yds/game to the WR2 role, above the ~36 norm.

Touchdown Board

Jake Ferguson is a live anytime-TD dart — WAS are leaky to tight ends in the end zone (0.35 TE TDs/game vs ~0.24).

CeeDee Lamb carries TD equity — WAS surrender 0.51 WR1 receiving scores a game.

Terry McLaurin carries TD equity — DAL surrender 0.59 WR1 receiving scores a game.

In the red zone DAL throw it (58% pass inside the 20) — CeeDee Lamb's TD equity over a goal-line back.

Game Script, Pace & Environment

A modest lean to DAL — they should lead more often than not, nudging them toward the run late and giving Javonte Williams a gentle game-script tailwind.

DAL — a balanced offense

DAL are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (44% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

Javonte Williams (13 carries, 53 yards projected) gets a mild game-script tailwind as a favorite, though DAL's willingness to keep throwing when ahead caps how much the lead converts into extra carries.

CeeDee Lamb projects for 7 targets and 57 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, Jake Ferguson (TE, 4 targets, 25 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

WAS — a run-heavy offense

WAS are one of the league's more run-committed offenses: on early downs while leading, they pass just 38% of the time, against a league average of 44% — a genuine clock-bleeding identity, not noise (it holds after shrinking their sample toward the league).

Game script works against the run here — WAS project to trail and throw, which squeezes Jacory Croskey-Merritt's rushing projection (11 carries, 49 yards) but raises his value as a receiver; trailing teams check the ball down, and his target share ticks up as the game gets away from them.

Terry McLaurin is the one to target from a volume standpoint: as underdogs throwing to keep pace, WAS funnel work to their top receiver — 6 targets for 51 yards projected, with genuine upside if they fall behind early and the game turns one-dimensional.

Underneath, Chig Okonkwo (TE, 5 targets, 34 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 4-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.

This preview and the projections below regenerate through the week as injuries, weather and line moves update the inputs.
